s.d: to cause to be deep
s.g: to make deep; to go deep

s.d: pertaining to being considerably below a surface
an extreme point on a scale of extent

s.dp: Know › Not Able To Be Known, Secret
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:βαθύς<SDBG:βαθύς:000000>}[a] ‘deep,’ {D:81.10}) the content of knowledge which is very difficult to know
s.g: deep secrets; secrets difficult to find out about
s.c: Only rarely can one use a literal rendering of τὰ βαθέα or τὰ βάθη in referring to secrets. In some instances it may be possible to use an expression such as ‘far away’ or ‘distant,’ and in other cases one can use expressions meaning ‘hard’ or ‘difficult.’ More often than not, however, the closest equivalent of τὰ βαθέα and τὰ βάθη in this type of context is either an expression of degree using a term such as ‘very’ (for example, ‘that which is very secret’) or an expression implying ‘that which is hidden’ or ‘that which is difficult to discover.’

s.d: branch of the palm tree (φοῖνιξ{N:001})
s.c: βάϊον is a technical term meaning ‘palm branch,’ and in ⟦John 12:13|John 12:13⟧ τῶν φοινίκων ‘of palm trees’ may have been added redundantly, since the term βάϊον may not have been regarded as sufficiently well known to readers.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a sorcerer and prophet summoned by Balak to curse Israel

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a king of Moab involved with Balaam
a receptacle for carrying money or other possessions; made of leather or cloth
to cause or to let fall down
to move down suddenly and quickly
s.g: to sweep down; to rush down
s.c: In a number of languages, however, it may be more appropriate to speak of a strong wind ‘blowing down from the island.’

s.dp: Activities Involving Liquids or Masses › Movement of Liquids or Masses
s.d: to cause a liquid to pour
to put or place some object or mass in a location, with the possible implication of force in some contexts
s.g: to put; to cause to be put

s.d: to cause a state or condition, with focus upon the suddenness or force of the action
to cause a state to cease by force and with the implication of elimination
s.g: to remove; to drive out; to do away with
s.c: In a number of languages it is extremely difficult to speak of states such as love and fear as being respectively agent and affected element. Therefore, it may be necessary to shift significantly the semantic structure so as to translate this expression in ⟦1 John 4:18|1 John 4:18⟧ as ‘if one completely loves, he does not at all fear.’

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Lend, Loan, Interest, Borrow, Bank
s.d: to deposit money with a banker, with the intent of earning interest
s.g: to deposit; to put in a bank

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to throw on a bed) to cause someone to become very ill
s.g: to cause illness; to make sick

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to throw into the heart) to cause someone to think in a particular manner, often as a means of inducing some behavior
s.g: to make think; to fill the heart; to cause to decide

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to throw a sickle) to begin to harvest a crop by cutting ripe grain with a sickle
s.g: to use a sickle; to swing a sickle; to begin to harvest
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 14:16|Revelation 14:16⟧ and ⟦Revelation 14:19|Revelation 14:19⟧ this idiom occurs in a figurative context, and therefore it may be necessary in some languages to speak of ‘harvesting’ rather than using a phrase which mentions the literal use of a sickle.

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to throw fire) to cause discord and contention
s.g: to cause discord; to cause division
s.c: Some translators have preferred to retain the literal rendering of this expression in ⟦Luke 12:49|Luke 12:49⟧, since this seems to be necessary in view of the larger figurative context, which speaks of ‘how I wish it were already kindled’ (τί θέλω εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη). A strictly literal translation may, however, be understood in a completely physical sense, namely, ‘to set the world on fire.’ There are a number of quite diverse interpretations of the significance of this expression in ⟦Luke 12:49|Luke 12:49⟧. Some have assumed, for example, that it refers to the fire of Pentecost.

s.d: to wash (in some contexts, possibly by dipping into water), with a view to making objects ritually acceptable
s.g: to wash; to purify; washing; purification
s.c: It is also possible to understand βαπτίσωνται in ⟦Mark 7:4|Mark 7:4⟧ as a middle form meaning ‘to wash themselves.’|There is some doubt as to the precise extent to which βαπτίζω, καταβαπτίζω, and βαπτισμός in ⟦Mark 7:4|Mark 7:4⟧ involve ritual cleansing, but the context would seem to imply this, particularly in view of the relationship of such washing to the rules followed by Jews in general and Pharisees in particular.

s.d: to employ water in a religious ceremony designed to symbolize purification and initiation on the basis of repentance{N:001}
s.c: According to the Didache (early second century) different forms of baptism were practiced in the early church, but with evident preference given to immersion.|The baptism practiced by John the Baptist would seem to reflect far more the Jewish pattern of ritual washing than the type of baptism employed by Christians, which constituted a symbol of initiation into the Christian community on the basis of belief in and loyalty to Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. There seems, however, to be no reason to employ a different expression for baptism in the case of John than in the case of the early Christians. Most translators actually employ a transliterated form of the Greek term βαπτίζω, but in some languages this is both awkward as well as inappropriate, especially if another term or expression has already been employed and is widely accepted by groups practicing various types or forms of baptism. In some languages, for example, one may employ an expression such as ‘to enter the water’ or ‘to undergo the ritual involving water.’ Such expressions do not necessarily imply the quantity of water nor the particular means by which water is applied.

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:βαπτίζω<SDBG:βαπτίζω:000001>}[b] ‘to baptize,’ {D:53.41}) to cause someone to have a highly significant religious experience involving special manifestations of God’s power and presence

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Pain, Suffering
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be baptized with a baptism) to be overwhelmed by some difficult experience or ordeal
s.c: It is usually not possible to employ the general term for ‘baptism’ to indicate a difficult trial or ordeal. On the other hand, there may be a serious problem involved in using a technical term for ‘ordeal,’ since such an expression may imply merely a ‘proof of innocence.’ In a number of languages, therefore, one can best translate the idiom simply as ‘to suffer greatly.’

s.d: to employ water in a religious ceremony designed to symbolize purification and initiation on the basis of repentance
s.c: According to the Didache (early second century) different forms of baptism were practiced in the early church, but with evident preference given to immersion.|The baptism practiced by John the Baptist would seem to reflect far more the Jewish pattern of ritual washing than the type of baptism employed by Christians, which constituted a symbol of initiation into the Christian community on the basis of belief in and loyalty to Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. There seems, however, to be no reason to employ a different expression for baptism in the case of John than in the case of the early Christians. In some languages, for example, one may employ an expression such as ‘to enter the water’ or ‘to undergo the ritual involving water.’ Such expressions do not necessarily imply the quantity of water nor the particular means by which water is applied.

s.d: to wash (in some contexts, possibly by dipping into water), with a view to making objects ritually acceptable
s.g: to wash; to purify; washing; purification
s.c: There is some doubt as to the precise extent to which βαπτίζω, καταβαπτίζω, and βαπτισμός in ⟦Mark 7:4|Mark 7:4⟧ involve ritual cleansing, but the context would seem to imply this, particularly in view of the relationship of such washing to the rules followed by Jews in general and Pharisees in particular.

s.d: (derivative of {L:βαπτίζω<SDBG:βαπτίζω:000001>}[b] ‘to baptize,’ {D:53.41}) one who baptizes

s.dp: Activities Involving Liquids or Masses › Use of Liquids
s.d: to dip an object in a liquid{N:001}

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a prisoner released by Pilate at the request of the Jews during the trial of Jesus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: an Israelite general

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the father of a man killed in the Temple

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Ethnic-Cultural
s.d: a person not participating in Greek culture and civilization (βάρβαρος contrasts with {L:Ἕλλην<SDBG:Ἕλλην:000000>}[a] ‘Greek,’ {D:11.90}, with the focus on culture rather than on language; see {S:04601401100024} at {D:11.94})
s.c: It would be a mistake in the case of ⟦Romans 1:14|Romans 1:14⟧ to speak merely of ‘Greeks and barbarians’ or ‘Greeks and savages.’ By NT times Ἕλλην (see LN 11.90) would have included most of those who participated in one way or another in the culture of the Greco-Roman world. Accordingly, one may render the contrast in ⟦Romans 1:14|Romans 1:14⟧ as ‘the civilized and the uncivilized.’

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Ethnic-Cultural
s.d: the native people of an area in which a language other than Greek or Latin was spoken (such persons would be regarded as being outside the civilized world of NT times)
s.c: In rendering this expression in ⟦Acts 28:2|Acts 28:2⟧ it would be possible in some languages to translate ‘the people there who spoke a strange language were friendly to us’ or ‘the local inhabitants of that island were kind to us.’ ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος καὶ ὁ λαλῶν ἐν ἐμοὶ βάρβαρος ‘I will be a foreigner to the one who speaks, and the one who speaks will be a foreigner to me’ ⟦1 Corinthians 14:11|1 Corinthians 14:11⟧. In ⟦1 Corinthians 14:11|1 Corinthians 14:11⟧ βάρβαρος implies being a foreigner from a country outside of the so-called civilized world.

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Particular Patterns of Behavior
s.d: a pattern of behavior associated with a low cultural level
s.c: Regardless of the level of culture or civilization, each ethnic group seems to be able to point to some other group regarded as being uncivilized. In some languages such a group is identified as ‘those who live far away’ or ‘those who do not live in towns’ or ‘those who are very strange.’ In ⟦Colossians 3:11|Colossians 3:11⟧ Σκύθης ‘Scythian’ (LN 93.583) may represent a state of civilization even lower than that implied by βάρβαρος ‘barbarian.’

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Experience Trouble, Hardship
s.d: to experience difficulty by burdensome and troublous obligations
s.g: to be burdened; to be troubled

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sleep, Waking
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be burdened by sleep) to be in a state of deep sleep
s.g: to be sound asleep; to be completely asleep

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sleep, Waking
s.d: (an idiom, literally: their eyes were weighed down) to become excessively or exceedingly sleepy
s.g: to have become very sleepy; to be very sleepy
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ἦσαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ βεβαρημένοι (or καταβαρυνόμενοι) would be ‘they could no longer keep their eyes open’ or ‘they could not drive sleep away.’

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to hear heavily with the ears) to be mentally slow or dull in comprehending
s.g: to be slow to understand; to be mentally dull

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: one of the twelve apostles

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a false prophet

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the ‘family name’ of the apostle Simon Peter

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: an additional name of a certain Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus who was an associate of Paul

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Trouble, Hardship, Distress
s.d: hardship which is regarded as particularly burdensome and exhausting
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 20:12|Matthew 20:12⟧ βάρος refers not to difficulties in general but to the specific hardship of working for the entire day.|In a number of languages hardship resulting from work may be expressed in terms of the effect upon the workers, for example, ‘to get tired from working’ or ‘to become weak as the result of working.’

s.d: a high point on a scale of extent and often implying importance and value

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the family name of a certain Joseph (often called Justus) who was one of two candidates for the place of Judas Iscariot

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the family name of a certain Judas who was appointed as a companion of Paul

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a blind man
pertaining to being relatively heavy
s.c: Although the meaning of βαρύς in ⟦Matthew 23:4|Matthew 23:4⟧ is literal, the entire expression is figurative, and so it may be necessary in some languages to say ‘they fix up heavy loads, so to speak, and tie them on people’s backs.’

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Difficult, Hard
s.d: pertaining to that which is difficult in view of its being burdensome
s.c: In rendering ‘his commandments are not burdensome,’ it may be necessary in some languages to translate ‘it is not difficult to do what he has commanded.’

s.d: pertaining to being important in view of substantive character
pertaining to one who is vicious and cruel
s.c: In a number of languages a strictly literal translation of ⟦Acts 20:29|Acts 20:29⟧ might be misunderstood. It may therefore be important to translate the last part of this expression as ‘people like cruel wolves will come among you.’

s.d: pertaining to being of great value or worth, implying in some contexts a monetary scale
to punish by physical torture or torment

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Pain, Suffering
s.d: severe pain associated with torture and torment
s.c: A strictly literal translation of ὁ καπνὸς τοῦ βασανισμοῦ αὐτῶν may be seriously misleading, for it might imply that it is the smoke which causes the suffering, but it is clearly the fire which torments them (as indicated in ⟦Revelation 14:10|Revelation 14:10⟧). Therefore, ir may be necessary to translate ‘and the smoke of the fire that torments them.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:βασανίζω<SDBG:βασανίζω:000000>} ‘to torture,’ {D:38.13}) a person serving as a guard in a prison, whose function was to torture prisoners as a phase of judicial examination
s.c: It is difficult to know in the case of ⟦Matthew 18:34|Matthew 18:34⟧ if βασανιστής is to be understood in the specific sense of ‘torturer’ (in which case it could be classified after LN 38.13) or only in terms of ‘prison guard.’ The use of βασανιστής in ⟦Matthew 18:34|Matthew 18:34⟧ may simply be an instance of literary hyperbole. As such it may be possible to translate the expression in ⟦Matthew 18:34|Matthew 18:34⟧ as ‘his master was very angry and handed him over to prison guards to torture him until he should pay back the whole amount.’

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Pain, Suffering
s.d: severe pain associated with torture and torment
the action of ruling as a king, with the implication of complete authority and the possibility of being able to pass on the right to rule to one’s son or near kin
s.c: It is generally a serious mistake to translate the phrase ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ‘the kingdom of God’ as referring to a particular area in which God rules. The meaning of this phrase in the NT involves not a particular place or special period of time but the fact of ruling. An expression such as ‘to enter the kingdom of God’ thus does not refer to ‘going to heaven’ but should be understood as ‘accepting God’s rule’ or ‘welcoming God to rule over.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Governmental Administrative Areas
s.d: an area or district ruled by a king
s.c: Since in many areas of the world kingship is not known (that is to say, the succession of rulers within a family and by inheritance), it may not be possible to find a technical term meaning ‘kingdom.’ Usually, however, one may employ an expression which is roughly equivalent in meaning to ‘domain,’ so that, for example, the last part of ⟦Mark 6:23|Mark 6:23⟧ may be rendered as ‘up to a half of the region which I rule.’

s.d: pertaining to a king
s.c: The expression ‘his royal robes’ may be rendered as ‘his clothing which he had as king,’ and the phrase ‘the royal priesthood’ may be rendered as ‘priests who are like kings.’

s.d: (ου n) the dwelling of a king or ruler; usually larger and more elaborate than the dwelling of an average person
s.c: In ⟦Luke 7:25|Luke 7:25⟧ βασίλειον may be rendered as ‘the home of a king’ or ‘the home of a ruler.’

s.d: one who has absolute authority within a particular area and is able to convey this power and authority to a successor (though in NT times, certain kings ruled only with the approval of Roman authorities and had no power to pass on their prerogatives)
to rule as a king, with the implication of complete authority and the possibility of being able to pass on the right to rule to one’s son or near kin
s.g: to rule; to be a king; to reign; rule; reign
s.c: It is generally a serious mistake to translate the phrase ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ‘the kingdom of God’ as referring to a particular area in which God rules. The meaning of this phrase in the NT involves not a particular place or special period of time but the fact of ruling. An expression such as ‘to enter the kingdom of God’ thus does not refer to ‘going to heaven’ but should be understood as ‘accepting God’s rule’ or ‘welcoming God to rule over.’

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:βασιλεύω<SDBG:βασιλεύω:000000>}[a] ‘to rule, to reign as a king,’ {D:37.64}) to be in control in an absolute manner
s.c: In a number of languages, however, it may be impossible to personify death as being capable of ‘reigning’ or ‘ruling.’ Sometimes the equivalent meaning may be expressed as ‘from the time of Adam to that of Moses there was no way for people to escape death’ or ‘… to die was certain’ (⟦Romans 5:14|Romans 5:14⟧).

s.d: pertaining to a king
s.c: The expression ‘his royal robes’ may be rendered as ‘his clothing which he had as king,’ and the phrase ‘the royal priesthood’ may be rendered as ‘priests who are like kings.’

s.d: an official directly responsible to a king
s.g: royal official; official of a king

s.d: a female ruler who has absolute authority within a particular area and who is able to pass on the power to rule to a successor{N:001}
s.c: For an analysis of the use of Κανδάκη in ⟦Acts 8:27|Acts 8:27⟧, see LN 37.77. See also LN 93.209.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the part of the leg below the ankle on which a person or animal stands and moves
s.c: βάσις is a more technical term for the foot than is πούς.

s.d: to bewitch a person, frequently by use of the evil eye and with evil intent
s.g: to bewitch; to practice magic on
s.c: βασκαίνω differs from μαγεύω to practice magic (LN 53.96) in that the former involves the use of so-called black magic, but for a different interpretation of βασκαίνω in ⟦Galatians 3:1|Galatians 3:1⟧, see LN 88.159.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Mislead, Lead Astray, Deceive
s.d: to deceive a person by devious and crafty means, with the possibility of a religious connotation in view of the literal meaning ‘to bewitch’ (see {D:53.98})
s.g: to deceive; to bewitch; to beguile
s.c: It is also possible that βασκαίνω in ⟦Galatians 3:1|Galatians 3:1⟧ is to be understood literally in the sense of bewitching by means of black magic (see LN 53.98).

s.d: to bear or carry a relatively heavy or burdensome object
to carry away from a place, with the probable implication of something that is relatively heavy
s.g: to remove; to carry away; to take away

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Patience, Endurance, Perseverance
s.d: (similar in meaning to {L:ὑποφέρω<SDBG:ὑποφέρω:000000>} ‘to endure,’ {D:25.175}, but probably somewhat more emphatic in meaning) to continue to bear up under unusually trying circumstances and difficulties
s.g: to endure; to bear up under

s.dp: Help, Care For › Provide For, Support
s.d: to provide continuous and possibly prolonged assistance and help by supplying the needs of someone
to undergo a grievous, difficult experience

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Accept As True
s.d: to accept, but with the implication of the truth being difficult to comprehend or to respond to properly
(an idiom, literally: to carry a name) to spread information extensively about a person
(an idiom, literally: to bear marks) to undergo experiences which mark one as the slave of some master
s.g: to bear the marks of a slave; to experience being the slave of
s.c: See also LN 8.55 and LN 33.481.

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Pain, Suffering
s.d: (a productive idiomatic expression, literally: to carry one’s cross) to be prepared to endure severe suffering, even to the point of death
s.g: to be prepared to suffer even unto death; to take up one’s cross
s.c: The idiom ‘to carry one’s cross’ or ‘to take up one’s cross’ involves a number of important features of meaning. Unfortunately, this expression is frequently not understood correctly by many people who hear it or even use it. One reason for this is the actual absence of crucifixion in modern society. If a literal translation is to be employed, then some marginal note will probably be necessary in order to indicate clearly the full implications of such a statement.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: (an idiom, literally: the womb carries) to experience the process of pregnancy
s.g: to be pregnant with; to carry in the womb
s.c: It may, however, be necessary in some languages to render ⟦Luke 11:27|Luke 11:27⟧ as ‘fortunate is the woman who gave you birth,’ since a literal reference to carrying in the womb may seem unduly crude.

s.dp: Plants › Plants That Are Not Trees
s.d: any kind of plant with sharp projections on its stem and/or branches; regarded as useless; symbol of hardship
s.c: The reference to the passage of Scripture in ⟦Luke 20:37|Luke 20:37⟧ is supplied from the context.|Except for ⟦Luke 6:44|Luke 6:44⟧, all occurrences of βάτος in the NT are to the burning bush of ⟦Exodus 3:2|Exodus 3:2⟧, in which the reference may very well be to a ‘burning thorn bush.’

s.dp: Spacial Dimensions › Specific Measures of Volume
s.d: a Hebrew liquid measure of between eight and nine gallons or approximately thirty-five liters
s.c: Because of the possible symbolic numerical values used in the Parable of the Dishonest Steward, it is important to retain the numerals, while making some adjustment in the case of the term βάτος. Accordingly, one may speak of ‘one hundred barrels of olive oil’ or ‘one hundred containers of olive oil’ or ‘one hundred large jars of olive oil.’

s.dp: Plants › Plants That Are Not Trees
s.d: any kind of plant with sharp projections on its stem and/or branches; regarded as useless; symbol of hardship
s.c: The reference to the passage of Scripture in ⟦Luke 20:37|Luke 20:37⟧ is supplied from the context.|Except for ⟦Luke 6:44|Luke 6:44⟧, all occurrences of βάτος in the NT are to the burning bush of ⟦Exodus 3:2|Exodus 3:2⟧, in which the reference may very well be to a ‘burning thorn bush.’

s.dp: Spacial Dimensions › Specific Measures of Volume
s.d: a Hebrew liquid measure of between eight and nine gallons or approximately thirty-five liters
s.c: Because of the possible symbolic numerical values used in the Parable of the Dishonest Steward, it is important to retain the numerals, while making some adjustment in the case of the term βάτος. Accordingly, one may speak of ‘one hundred barrels of olive oil’ or ‘one hundred containers of olive oil’ or ‘one hundred large jars of olive oil.’

s.d: tailless amphibian with a squat body, moist smooth skin, and long hind legs for jumping; about 70 mm long; brown or olive-green; develops from tadpole; Rana esculenta (Edible frog) or Rana punctata (Spotted frog)
s.c: In this only reference to frogs in the NT, the connotation is of something unclean and abhorrent. In a number of societies, however, frogs are regarded as very valuable and worthwhile animals, since they are often an important source of food. On the other hand, in such areas there are usually certain types of frogs or toads which are particularly poisonous and whose names, therefore, do carry bad connotations.

s.d: to speak much or extensively, with a possible added implication of meaningless words
s.g: to use many words; to speak for a long time
s.c: For another interpretation of βατταλογέω in ⟦Matthew 6:7|Matthew 6:7⟧, see βατταλογέω LN 33.89.

s.d: to utter senseless sounds or to speak indistinctly and incoherently
s.c: For another interpretation of βατταλογέω in ⟦Matthew 6:7|Matthew 6:7⟧, see βατταλογέω LN 33.88.|In some languages the equivalent of ‘to babble’ is ‘to speak like a baby’ or ‘to speak sounds that make no sense.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:βδελύσσομαι<SDBG:βδελύσσομαι:000000>}  ‘to abhor,’ {D:25.186}) that which is utterly detestable and abhorrent
s.g: what is detestable; what is abhorrent

s.d: (a fixed phrase derived from Hebrew, literally: the detestable thing of desolation) an abomination (either an object or an event) which defiles a holy place and thus causes it to be abandoned and left desolate
s.g: an abomination which desolates; a horrible thing which defiles
s.c: In translating βδέλυγμα, it may be necessary in some languages to use a phrase such as ‘that which God detests’ or ‘that which God hates’ or even ‘that which causes God’s anger.’ The term ἐρημώσεως may then be translated as ‘that which causes people to abandon’ or ‘that which causes something to be deserted.’ The entire phrase may then be translated in some languages as ‘that which God detests and which causes something to be abandoned’ or ‘… left desolate.’

s.d: pertaining to one who or that which is or should be detested or regarded as abhorrent
s.c: In some languages ‘detestable’ may be rendered as ‘thought to be extremely bad’ or even ‘that which should never even be seen.’

s.d: to strongly detest something on the basis that it is abominable
s.c: It is possible that in ⟦Revelation 21:8|Revelation 21:8⟧ ἐβδελυγμένοις refers to sexual perverts.

s.d: pertaining to being certain, on the basis of being well established

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Trust, Rely
s.d: pertaining to being able to be relied on or depended on
s.c: For another interpretation of βέβαιος in ⟦Hebrews 2:2|Hebrews 2:2⟧, see βέβαιος LN 28.43.

s.c: For another interpretation of βεβαιόω in ⟦Mark 16:20|Mark 16:20⟧, see βεβαιόω LN 31.91.

s.d: to increase in inner strength, with the implication of greater firmness of character or attitude

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed

s.g: to confirm; to verify; to prove to be true and certain; confirmation; verification
s.c: ⟦Philippians 1:7|Philippians 1:7⟧ βεβαίωσις may denote either the process of making known something in such a way as to confirm its truth or the process of causing people to think about something and to accept it as trustworthy, in which case βεβαίωσις might also be classified in Domain 31 Hold a View, Believe, Trust, Subdomain G Accept as True.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Bad, Evil, Harmful, Damaging
s.d: pertaining to being profane in the sense of worldly or godless
to cause something to become unclean, profane, or ritually unacceptable{N:001}
s.g: to make unclean; to defile; to profane
s.c: In a number of languages it is quite impossible to translate literally the concept of ‘unclean,’ for physical cleanliness and ritual acceptability are completely unrelated. In some languages it is necessary to translate κοινόω or βεβηλόω as ‘to take away its holiness’ or ‘to make something unacceptable to God.’ In many cultures one must express this concept as involving so-called negative taboo.

a raised platform mounted by steps and usually furnished with a seat; used by officials to address an assembly, often on judicial matters, with a focus on judgement
s.c: The association of a βῆμα with judicial procedures means that there is almost always an important component of judicial function associated with this term. Therefore in translating βῆμα, it is often best to use a phrase such as ‘a place where a judge decides’ or ‘a place where decisions are made’ or ‘a judge’s seat.’ The focus upon judgment is particularly important in those passages which refer to the judgment seat of God (⟦Romans 14:10|Romans 14:10⟧) and of Christ (⟦2 Corinthians 5:10|2 Corinthians 5:10⟧).

s.d: (an idiom, literally: a step of a foot (a distance of approximately two and a half feet or a little less than a meter)) an extremely limited or restricted space

a strong, destructive force
s.c: In some languages it is difficult, if not impossible, to find a term such as ‘violence,’ but one may describe the effects of violence by expressions which indicate the harm that is done. For example, ⟦Acts 5:26|Acts 5:26⟧ may be translated ‘they did not wish to harm anyone, for they were afraid of the people,’ and similarly in ⟦Acts 27:41|Acts 27:41⟧, one may translate ‘the waves did great damage to the stern.’

s.d: to experience a violent attack
s.g: to be attacked with violence; to suffer violent attacks
s.c: In many languages it may be difficult, if not impossible, to speak of the kingdom of heaven ‘suffering violent attacks,’ but generally some active form may be employed, for example, ‘and violently attack the kingdom of heaven’ or ‘ … the rule of God.’ See comment at βιάζω LN 20.10.

s.d: to employ violence in doing harm to someone or something
s.c: Since there are a number of different interpretations of this expression (πᾶς εἰς αὐτὴν βιάζεται) in ⟦Luke 16:16|Luke 16:16⟧ as well as for the parallel expression in ⟦Matthew 11:12|Matthew 11:12⟧ (ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν βιάζεται; see βιάζω); it is important to consult various commentaries before undertaking a translation. Probably the most widely held interpretation of these difficult expressions is based on the fact that many people did not hesitate to employ violence or military force in order to establish what they regarded as the rule of God on earth.

s.d: pertaining to the use of violent or strong force
(derivative of βιάζομαι[b] ‘to use violence,’ {D:20.10}) a person who employs violence in order to accomplish his purpose
s.c: See the comment at LN 20.10 for a discussion of some of the problems involved in the interpretation of this type of expression.

s.c: There is no indication in ⟦1 Timothy 6:9|1 Timothy 6:9⟧ as to the specific nature of the harm, but the extent of it is made clear in the following clause which speaks of complete destruction. This could be physical, moral, and/or spiritual.

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Harm, Wound

s.c: In translating terms meaning ‘to harm’ or ‘to injure,’ it may be necessary to specify suffering, for example, ‘to cause people to suffer’ or ‘to cause people to have pain.’

s.c: The initial stages of growth, either of a plant as a whole or in the renewal of foliage after a winter or dry season, may be expressed in a number of ways, for example, ‘to become green again,’ ‘to show leaves,’ ‘to see leaves begin,’ or ‘when leaves unfold.’

to speak against someone in such a way as to harm or injure his or her reputation (occurring in relation to persons as well as to divine beings)

s.c: One way in which βλασφημέω and βλασφημία were used in speaking of defaming God was by claiming some kind of equality with God. Any such statement was regarded by the Jews of biblical times as being harmful and injurious to the nature of God.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Depressions and Holes

s.c: In a number of languages a distinction is made between ditches dug by people for presumably agricultural purposes and those which are natural depressions in the ground. There is no way to determine from the NT contexts which type of ditch is involved.
